title: MODULE 11 — Next.js and Modern Web Application Architecture

overview.text: Module overview

Next.js is a React framework used to build production-grade web applications. It provides routing, server-side rendering, static generation, server-side data fetching, caching, image optimization, metadata management, and deployment capabilities.

In this module, you will progress from understanding Next.js fundamentals to designing a complete application architecture that can support real-world traffic, dynamic content, search-engine indexing, and scalable development.
What you will learn
By the end of this module, you should be able to:
Understand how Next.js extends React.
Create production-ready Next.js applications using TypeScript.
Design an application using the App Router.
Build static, dynamic, and nested routes.
Design reusable layouts and navigation systems.
Understand Server Components and Client Components.
Choose the appropriate rendering strategy for different pages.
Implement SSR, SSG, and ISR.
Understand hydration and the React rendering lifecycle.
Fetch, cache, and revalidate application data.
Implement streaming and Suspense.
Build SEO-friendly pages with dynamic metadata.
Optimize images, fonts, and application performance.
Implement production-grade error and loading interfaces.
Deploy and understand the architecture of a Next.js application.
How the lessons fit together
Next.js foundations — Lessons 1–3: Framework architecture, TypeScript and project structure.
Routing and application architecture — Lessons 4–5: Dynamic routes, layouts and navigation.
React rendering architecture — Lessons 6–10: Server Components, rendering strategies and hydration.
Data and performance engineering — Lessons 11–12: Data fetching, caching, streaming and Suspense.
SEO and production readiness — Lessons 13–16: Metadata, optimization, error handling and deployment.

sections.title: Introduction to Next.js and React Framework Architecture

blocks.text: 1.1 What is Next.js?
Next.js is a React-based web framework that provides the infrastructure required to build complete web applications.
To understand why Next.js exists, first understand what React does.
React is primarily a user-interface library. It gives developers tools to create components, manage state, and build interactive interfaces.
However, a production web application needs much more than components.
For example, consider building an educational platform like PrepSpaces.
It might contain:
A homepage.
Course listing pages.
Individual course pages.
Student dashboards.
Authentication pages.
Dynamic lesson pages.
Search-engine-friendly content pages.
Administrative interfaces.
With React alone, you need to make many additional architectural decisions and integrate different tools.
Next.js provides an integrated framework for many of these requirements.
1.2 React vs Next.js
Capability | React alone | Next.js
UI components | Yes | Yes
Component state | Yes | Yes
File-based routing | External library needed | Built in
Server rendering | Additional setup | Built in
Static generation | Additional setup | Built in
Server Components | React infrastructure/setup | Integrated
Metadata management | Manual or external tools | Built in
Image optimization | External solution | Built in
Route-level loading UI | Custom implementation | Built-in conventions
Deployment | Depends on chosen stack | Framework-aware deployment
React is the foundation for building the UI. Next.js adds application-level architecture around React.
1.3 Understanding traditional React architecture
In a typical client-rendered React application, the browser downloads JavaScript, executes the application and renders the interface.
Consider the process:

User opens website
       ↓
Browser requests application
       ↓
HTML and JavaScript downloaded
       ↓
JavaScript executes
       ↓
React renders components
       ↓
User sees application
This architecture is commonly known as Client-Side Rendering (CSR).
One potential disadvantage is that the browser may need to execute JavaScript before the meaningful page content is available.
The actual experience depends on how the application is built, how much JavaScript it downloads, and whether it uses prerendering.
1.4 Understanding Next.js architecture
Next.js can render content on the server, generate pages ahead of time, or combine server-generated and client-rendered interfaces.

User
               ↓
            Browser
               ↓
      Next.js Application
        ┌──────┴──────┐
        ↓             ↓
     Server        Client
   Rendering     Interaction
        ↓             ↓
  Database/API    React UI
        └──────┬──────┘
               ↓
      Complete Interface
The server can retrieve data and render content before the browser receives the page. The browser can then hydrate the interactive Client Components.
1.5 Important features of Next.js
1. File-based routing: Your folder structure determines your application URLs.
2. Server Components: Components can execute on the server and retrieve data without sending their component implementation to the browser.
3. Client Components: Components can provide browser-based functionality such as buttons, forms, event handling, and interactive dashboards.
4. Rendering strategies: Next.js supports different rendering approaches depending on whether content is static, dynamic, or periodically updated.
5. Data fetching: Server Components can retrieve information from APIs, databases, and other server-side sources.
6. Optimization: Next.js provides built-in facilities for image handling, font loading, code splitting, and navigation prefetching.
1.6 When should you use Next.js?
Next.js is particularly useful for:
Educational platforms.
E-commerce applications.
SaaS platforms.
Blogs and publishing systems.
Business websites.
Documentation platforms.
Job portals.
Content-driven applications.
Applications requiring a combination of public SEO pages and private dashboards.
For example, a learning platform can use server rendering for publicly accessible course pages and authenticated, dynamic content for its student dashboard.
Lesson outcome: You should understand why a React framework is useful, how Next.js extends React, and which application requirements it addresses.
This lesson teaches you how to initialize a Next.js application, configure the development environment, and establish a maintainable TypeScript codebase.
2.1 Understanding the development environment
Before creating a Next.js application, you need to understand the tools involved.
Technology | Responsibility
Node.js | Runs JavaScript outside the browser
npm | Manages project dependencies
Next.js | Provides the React application framework
React | Builds the user interface
TypeScript | Adds static type checking
ESLint | Helps identify code-quality problems
Git | Tracks project changes
You should also understand the difference between a development environment and a production environment.
Development environment: Used to write code, test functionality, and identify errors.
Production environment: Used to serve the optimized application to real users.
2.2 Creating a Next.js application
Run:
npx create-next-app@latest my-platform
You will be prompted to configure several project options, including:
TypeScript.
ESLint.
Tailwind CSS.
App Router.
Import aliases.
Optional project-directory preferences.
For this course, select TypeScript and App Router.
Navigate into the project:
cd my-platform
Start the development server:
npm run dev
Open: http://localhost:3000 — Your Next.js development server is now running.
2.3 Understanding package.json
The package.json file contains project information, dependencies and scripts.
Example:
Command | Purpose
npm run dev | Starts development mode
npm run build | Builds the production application
npm run start | Starts the production server
npm run lint | Runs configured lint checks
The exact scripts may differ between project templates and package versions.
2.4 What is TypeScript?
JavaScript is dynamically typed, meaning variables do not require predefined types.

let age = 21;
age = "Student";
JavaScript allows this assignment.
TypeScript introduces static type checking.
TypeScript helps catch incorrect data usage during development.
2.5 TypeScript in React components
Consider a reusable course card.
Here:
Course describes the structure of course information.
CourseCardProps defines the properties accepted by the component.
CourseCard receives strongly typed data.
This makes components more predictable and maintainable.
2.6 Understanding project configuration
Students should understand the purpose of:
tsconfig.json: TypeScript compiler configuration.
next.config.ts: Next.js configuration.
eslint.config.mjs: ESLint configuration.
.gitignore: Files excluded from version control.
.env.local: Local environment variables.
package-lock.json: Locked dependency versions.
2.7 Environment variables
Applications frequently connect to external APIs and databases.
You should not place private credentials directly inside source code.
Example:

DATABASE_URL=your_database_url
API_SECRET=your_secret
NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=https://api.example.com
Access server-side environment variables using:
const databaseUrl = process.env.DATABASE_URL;
Variables beginning with NEXT_PUBLIC_ can be exposed to the browser. Never put passwords, private API credentials, or database secrets in them.
Lesson outcome: You should be able to initialize a Next.js TypeScript project, configure the development environment, create typed React components, and manage project configuration safely.
3.1 What is the App Router?
The App Router is Next.js's modern routing architecture. It uses the application's file and folder structure to define routes.
It is built around modern React features, including Server Components and Suspense.
The App Router is different from the older Pages Router, which uses the pages/ directory.
This course focuses on the App Router.
3.2 Understanding the project structure
Consider the following project:

my-platform/
├── app/
│   ├── layout.tsx
│   ├── page.tsx
│   ├── globals.css
│   ├── courses/
│   │   ├── page.tsx
│   │   └── [slug]/
│   │       └── page.tsx
│   ├── dashboard/
│   │   ├── layout.tsx
│   │   └── page.tsx
│   ├── about/
│   │   └── page.tsx
│   └── api/
│       └── courses/
│           └── route.ts
├── components/
│   ├── Navbar.tsx
│   ├── Footer.tsx
│   └── CourseCard.tsx
├── lib/
│   ├── database.ts
│   └── courses.ts
├── public/
│   └── images/
├── types/
│   └── course.ts
├── next.config.ts
├── tsconfig.json
└── package.json
Let's understand the important directories.
1. app/: Contains route definitions, pages, layouts, loading interfaces and error interfaces.
2. components/: Contains reusable UI components such as navigation bars, buttons, cards and forms.
3. lib/: Contains shared application logic, data access functions, database connections and utilities.
4. public/: Contains static assets such as logos, images, icons and other publicly accessible files.
5. types/: Contains reusable TypeScript types and interfaces.
This separation makes a large application easier to maintain.
3.3 Understanding special App Router files
Next.js recognizes specific filenames and assigns them special functionality.
File | Responsibility
page.tsx | Creates a route's page
layout.tsx | Creates a shared layout
template.tsx | Creates a layout-like structure with a new instance during navigation
loading.tsx | Provides a loading interface
error.tsx | Handles errors in a route segment
not-found.tsx | Displays a not-found interface
route.ts | Defines an API endpoint or route handler
global-error.tsx | Handles errors at the root level
globals.css | Contains global styles
These conventions allow Next.js to coordinate routing and rendering automatically.
3.4 Understanding page.tsx
A page.tsx file creates the actual page associated with a URL.
Example: app/page.tsx
This creates the homepage: http://localhost:3000/
Now create: app/courses/page.tsx
This creates: http://localhost:3000/courses
Notice that the folder name determines the URL segment.
3.5 Understanding root layout
The root layout is the shared foundation of the application.
app/layout.tsx
The root layout contains elements shared across pages, including the HTML document structure.
For example, your navigation bar, global providers and common application wrappers may be placed here or in nested layouts, depending on their scope.
3.6 Organizing a large project
A common mistake is putting every component, API call and utility inside the app/ directory.
A cleaner architecture separates responsibilities:

Application
├── Routing (Pages, Layouts, Loading, Errors)
├── Components (Common UI, Forms, Course Components)
├── Business Logic (Data Services, Database, Utilities)
└── Types (Interfaces, Data Models)
Lesson outcome: Understand how the App Router recognizes routes, how its special files work, and how to structure a maintainable Next.js project.
Routing determines which page is displayed when a user visits a particular URL.
4.1 Understanding file-based routing
Traditional routing often requires manually defining URL-to-component mappings.
In Next.js App Router, folders and special files determine the routes.

app/
├── page.tsx
├── about/
│   └── page.tsx
├── contact/
│   └── page.tsx
└── courses/
    └── page.tsx
File location | URL
app/page.tsx | /
app/about/page.tsx | /about
app/contact/page.tsx | /contact
app/courses/page.tsx | /courses
The important concept is that a folder by itself does not create a publicly accessible page. A route becomes a page when it contains a page.tsx file.
4.2 What are dynamic routes?
Suppose your platform contains 100 courses.
You could manually create 100 separate page files, but this would be difficult to maintain.
Instead, dynamic routing allows a single page template to display different content based on the URL.
Example: app/courses/[slug]/page.tsx
This route can handle: /courses/react, /courses/javascript, /courses/python, /courses/system-design.
The [slug] segment is a dynamic route parameter.
4.3 Accessing route parameters
Example:
An important modern Next.js detail: route params are asynchronous in current App Router conventions, so you should await them. Older tutorials may show synchronous access.
4.4 Dynamic route types
There are several ways to define dynamic segments.
Single dynamic segment: app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx (e.g. /blog/nextjs, /blog/react, /blog/typescript)
Multiple dynamic segments: app/courses/[courseId]/lessons/[lessonId]/page.tsx (e.g. /courses/101/lessons/5)
Catch-all routes: app/docs/[...slug]/page.tsx (e.g. /docs/frontend, /docs/frontend/react, /docs/frontend/react/hooks)
Optional catch-all routes: app/docs/[[...slug]]/page.tsx (can also match /docs without requiring a slug)
4.5 Query parameters
Dynamic route segments are not the same as query parameters.
Consider: /courses?category=frontend&level=advanced
Here category and level are query parameters, not part of the pathname.
Query parameters are useful for Search, Filtering, Pagination, Sorting, and Category selection.

4.6 Generating routes at build time
Next.js provides generateStaticParams() to identify dynamic paths that can be generated during the build.
Example:
Next.js can use these parameters to prerender the specified dynamic pages.
You will study this more deeply in the Static Site Generation lesson.
Lesson outcome: You should be able to create static routes, dynamic routes, nested URL structures, catch-all routes, and query-based filtering systems.
A production application usually contains multiple pages that share the same design and interface elements.
For example, an educational platform may contain:
A common navigation bar.
A common footer.
A sidebar.
A dashboard header.
A shared course navigation system.
You should not need to recreate these elements independently for every page.
Next.js provides layouts and templates to solve this problem.
5.1 What is a layout?
A layout is a reusable UI structure surrounding the content of one or more pages.
Example: app/layout.tsx
Every route using this root layout receives the same shared application structure.
5.2 What are nested layouts?
A large application may contain different sections with different designs.

app/
├── layout.tsx
├── page.tsx
├── dashboard/
│   ├── layout.tsx
│   ├── page.tsx
│   ├── courses/
│   │   └── page.tsx
│   └── settings/
│       └── page.tsx
└── courses/
    └── page.tsx
The dashboard layout applies to /dashboard, /dashboard/courses, and /dashboard/settings.
It can contain a sidebar, student profile navigation and dashboard-specific navigation.
The other routes can use the root layout without the dashboard sidebar.
5.3 Layout composition

Root Layout
├── Main Navbar
├── Dashboard Layout
│   ├── Dashboard Sidebar
│   └── Dashboard Page
└── Footer
Nested layouts are composed automatically by Next.js.
5.4 What is a template?
A template is similar to a layout, but it creates a new component instance when users navigate between certain route segments.
Layouts: Preserve their component state during navigation, avoid unnecessary remounting, and are suitable for persistent interface elements.
Templates: Create a fresh instance when their segment is navigated, can reset component state, and can be useful when an animation, effect or component initialization should run again.
For example, a persistent dashboard sidebar is generally better suited to a layout than a template.
5.5 Navigation using Link
Next.js provides the Link component.
The Link component provides optimized client-side navigation and can prefetch routes when appropriate.
This can reduce the waiting time when users move between pages.
5.6 Route groups
Route groups allow developers to organize related routes without adding the group name to the URL.

app/
├── (marketing)/
│   ├── about/
│   │   └── page.tsx
│   └── pricing/
│       └── page.tsx
├── (authentication)/
│   ├── login/
│   │   └── page.tsx
│   └── register/
│       └── page.tsx
└── layout.tsx
The URLs remain /about, /pricing, /login, /register. The parentheses are not included in the URL.
Route groups are useful for organizing applications with different interface requirements.
5.7 Practical architecture example
Section | Layout requirements
Public homepage | Navbar and footer
Course catalogue | Public navigation
Course details | Public navigation and course information
Student dashboard | Sidebar and dashboard navigation
Lesson interface | Course sidebar and learning content
Authentication | Simplified authentication layout
Your task is to design the route hierarchy and decide which elements should persist across navigation.
Lesson outcome: Understand shared layouts, nested layouts, templates, route groups, and optimized navigation.
This is one of the most important lessons in modern Next.js.
To build efficient applications, you must understand where React components execute, why some components run on the server, and why others need to run inside the browser.
6.1 Understanding the two environments
A Next.js application works across two primary environments.

Server environment: Access databases, communicate with private APIs, read server-side environment variables, retrieve protected information, generate page content, execute server-side application logic.
Client environment: Respond to button clicks, manage interactive states, display animations, access browser APIs, read browser storage, manage client-side forms and interactions.
These environments have different responsibilities.
6.2 What are Server Components?
Server Components are React components that execute on the server.
In the App Router, layouts and pages are Server Components by default.
Example: app/courses/page.tsx
Notice that the component is asynchronous. It retrieves course information before returning the rendered interface.
Important characteristics:
Server Components can retrieve information from databases and APIs.
Their component implementation does not need to be included in the browser's JavaScript bundle.
They can access server-only resources.
They cannot directly use browser-only APIs.
They cannot use interactive React hooks such as useState and useEffect.
6.3 What are Client Components?
Client Components are components that participate in browser-side interactivity.
To create a Client Component, use the "use client" directive at the top of the file.
Example:
Client Components support: useState, useEffect, useReducer, event handlers, browser APIs, interactive forms, client-side navigation hooks, animations and interactive UI libraries.
6.4 Server Components vs Client Components
Feature | Server Component | Client Component
Default in App Router | Yes | No
Server-side data access | Yes | Through APIs or passed data
useState | No | Yes
useEffect | No | Yes
Browser APIs | No | Yes
Event handlers | No | Yes
Server secrets | Yes, in server-only code | Never directly
Browser JavaScript required for component logic | No | Yes
6.5 Understanding the component boundary

Course Page (Server Component)
├── Course Information
├── Course Description
├── Course Syllabus
├── Enrolment Button (Client)
└── Progress Tracker (Client)
This avoids turning the entire course page into a Client Component unnecessarily.
6.6 Building a combined component
Server Component: app/courses/[slug]/page.tsx
Client Component: components/EnrolButton.tsx
The example only changes local UI state; an actual enrolment system must also save and verify enrolment on the server.
6.7 Understanding the RSC Payload
React Server Components use a representation called the React Server Component Payload (RSC Payload).
It contains information about:
The rendered Server Component tree.
Placeholders for Client Components.
References to the JavaScript needed by those Client Components.
Props passed between components.
On the initial load, Next.js uses the RSC Payload and Client Component code to generate an HTML preview. The browser then hydrates the Client Components.
On later navigations, Next.js can use RSC data to update the interface without downloading and reconstructing the entire application from scratch. (Next.js)
6.8 Common mistakes
Mistake 1: Using "use client" everywhere. This unnecessarily increases the amount of JavaScript sent to the browser.
Mistake 2: Accessing window inside a Server Component. The window object exists in the browser, not in the server environment.
Mistake 3: Trying to fetch private database information directly from a Client Component. Database credentials and private business logic should remain server-side.

Mistake 4: Passing non-serializable values across the Server-to-Client boundary. Ordinary component props crossing this boundary should use supported serializable values. You cannot simply pass an ordinary server-defined callback as an event handler to a Client Component.
Lesson outcome: You should be able to design applications that combine Server Components and Client Components while minimizing unnecessary browser JavaScript.
7.1 What is Server-Side Rendering?
Server-Side Rendering is a rendering approach in which the server generates HTML for a page in response to a request.
The browser receives the generated HTML instead of having to construct the entire initial page from JavaScript alone.

Consider a student visiting /courses/react: the server receives the request, identifies the route, retrieves the required course information, renders the page, and sends the generated response to the browser.
7.2 CSR vs SSR
Client-Side Rendering (CSR): Browser requests the application -> JavaScript is downloaded -> React executes in the browser -> Components render and content becomes visible.

Server-Side Rendering (SSR): Browser requests the page -> Server retrieves required information -> Server generates HTML -> Browser displays the returned HTML -> Client Components hydrate for interaction.
7.3 Why is SSR useful?
SSR is useful when page content depends on information that should be retrieved at request time:
Personalized dashboards.
Authenticated student interfaces.
Pages using request-specific information.
Frequently changing data.
Content that must reflect the latest server-side state.

SSR can also improve the initial delivery of meaningful content compared with a purely client-rendered page, depending on the implementation. However, SSR is not automatically faster in every situation. It adds server processing and may introduce request latency.
7.4 How to implement request-time rendering
Because this page accesses request-specific cookie data, it cannot be fully generated as one identical static page for all requests.
In a real application, the session must be validated securely on the server before showing private information.
7.5 Understanding request-time rendering
Compare two pages:
Example A: Public course description — changes only when an administrator updates the course; can be generated ahead of time and cached.
Example B: Student dashboard — depends on the current student's authenticated session and progress; needs request-specific data.
This is why production applications frequently combine different rendering strategies.
7.6 SSR does not mean every Server Component renders on every request
This is an important distinction.
A Server Component can participate in a page that was prerendered at build time. Being a Server Component does not automatically mean it runs on every incoming request.
Rendering strategy and component execution environment are related but different concepts.
Lesson outcome: Understand request-time HTML generation, personalized server rendering, the differences between CSR and SSR, and when SSR is appropriate.
8.1 What is Static Site Generation?
Static Site Generation (SSG) is a rendering approach in which pages are generated ahead of time rather than individually rendered for every incoming visitor.
The generated HTML can then be served repeatedly.
Consider a documentation platform containing 500 articles. If those articles are mostly the same for all visitors, generating them beforehand can reduce the work required to serve each request.
8.2 How SSG works

Source Code
     ↓
Next.js Build
     ↓
Data Retrieval
     ↓
Page Generation
     ↓
Static HTML Files
     ↓
CDN / Host
     ↓
Visitors
8.3 Static rendering example
A page with stable content can be eligible for prerendering.
8.4 SSG with dynamic routes
For app/courses/[slug]/page.tsx:
Next.js can generate these specified routes during the build. The actual page content is then retrieved using the corresponding slug.
8.5 SSG vs SSR
Feature | SSG | SSR
HTML generation | Ahead of time | At request time
Server work per visitor | Usually lower | Required for dynamic rendering
Best for | Stable public content | Request-specific content
CDN delivery | Straightforward | Depends on response and caching
Personalization | Not directly in shared static HTML | Can use request-specific data
Content freshness | Depends on rebuild or revalidation | Can retrieve current data per request
8.6 Where should you use SSG?
SSG is particularly useful for:
Documentation.
Public course descriptions.
Blog articles.
Product descriptions.
Company information.
Public landing pages.
Frequently accessed pages with relatively stable content.
It is less suitable when the entire page must be personalized for each request.
8.7 Understanding prerendering
Prerendering means preparing the page output before the visitor requests it.
SSG is an important form of prerendering.
Do not confuse prerendering with caching: prerendering creates output ahead of time, whereas caching controls whether previously generated output or data can be reused.
Lesson outcome: Understand build-time page generation, dynamic-route prerendering, the purpose of generateStaticParams(), and when static rendering is more suitable than request-time rendering.
9.1 What is ISR?
Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) allows a Next.js application to update previously generated pages without requiring a complete application rebuild for every content change.
It combines the benefits of static generation with the ability to refresh content over time.
9.2 Understanding the ISR lifecycle

First Page Generation
         ↓
   Store Output
         ↓
  Serve Cached Page
         ↓
Revalidation Condition
         ↓
Regenerate Page Output
         ↓
  Store Updated Output
         ↓
  Serve Fresh Version

With time-based ISR, an expired or stale cached page can be served while regeneration occurs in the background. The regenerated result replaces the previously cached output after successful completion. (Next.js)
9.3 Time-based revalidation
In the classic App Router caching model, you can configure time-based revalidation.
The value 3600 represents 3,600 seconds, or one hour. This is an upper-bound freshness interval, not a guarantee that the page regenerates exactly at the one-hour mark.
9.4 On-demand revalidation
Next.js provides revalidatePath() and revalidateTag().
Example using path-based revalidation:
This invalidates the relevant cached route so that a subsequent request can obtain regenerated output.
9.5 Understanding tag-based revalidation
You can associate tags with cached data and invalidate data using those tags (e.g. courses, course-101) without unnecessarily invalidating unrelated course data.
9.6 Modern Next.js caching: an important version distinction
The caching APIs and defaults have evolved. The current documentation describes two approaches:
Approach A: Previous caching model — Without Cache Components enabled, you can use the traditional route-segment revalidate configuration, fetch caching options, and on-demand revalidation.
Approach B: Cache Components — Introduced in Next.js 16, enabled using:
You can then use "use cache", cacheLife(), cacheTag(), revalidateTag(), updateTag(), and revalidatePath().
Example:

The caching configuration should be chosen deliberately for the project's Next.js version. Do not mix examples from the previous caching model with Cache Components without understanding their different semantics. (Next.js)
9.7 Where should you use ISR?
Application content | Suitable strategy
Public blog articles | Static generation with revalidation
Course descriptions | Static generation with revalidation
Product catalogue | Static generation with revalidation
Frequently updated news | Shorter revalidation or dynamic rendering
Private student dashboard | Request-specific rendering
Live user activity | Dynamic or client-side data updates
Lesson outcome: Understand ISR, stale content, regeneration, cache invalidation, and the difference between the classic caching model and modern Cache Components.
This lesson connects everything you have learned about server rendering and Client Components.
10.1 What is hydration?
Hydration is the process through which React attaches client-side functionality to HTML that has already been generated by the server.
10.2 Understanding the complete rendering lifecycle
The initial HTML can contain the text Like. The browser can display that button immediately, and the click interaction becomes functional after hydration.
10.3 Step-by-step hydration process

User Requests Page
       ↓
  Next.js Server
       ↓
Render Server Components -> Generate RSC Payload -> Generate Initial HTML
       ↓
Browser Receives HTML -> Content Displayed
       ↓
Client Component JavaScript -> Hydration -> Interactive Components
Next.js coordinates the HTML preview, RSC Payload and Client Component JavaScript to provide this experience. (Next.js)
10.4 What is a hydration mismatch?
A hydration mismatch happens when React encounters a difference between the server-generated output and the initial browser-side rendering.
Example:
Other common causes include:
Using Math.random() during rendering.
Reading localStorage directly during the initial render.
Accessing browser-only information before hydration.
Invalid HTML nesting.
Rendering different content based on inconsistent server and client state.
Date or number formatting differences.
10.5 How to prevent hydration mismatches
Browser-specific data that is not available on the server should generally be read after the component mounts.
10.6 Hydration vs rendering
Concept | Meaning
Rendering | Producing the UI representation
Server rendering | Producing the initial output on the server
Client rendering | Rendering UI in the browser
Hydration | Attaching React functionality to server-generated HTML
Reconciliation | React comparing UI changes and updating the rendered interface
10.7 Why hydration matters for performance
The user experience has two important milestones: Content visibility and Interactivity.

A large Client Component bundle may delay interactivity even when the server-generated HTML is already visible. Minimizing unnecessary Client Components, reducing JavaScript and using appropriate component boundaries matter.
Lesson outcome: Understand how Next.js generates HTML, how RSC Payload works, how hydration activates interactive components, and how to diagnose hydration mismatch problems.

sections.title: Data Fetching and Caching in Next.js

blocks.text: 11.1 Understanding data fetching
Data fetching means retrieving information from a data source (REST APIs, GraphQL APIs, SQL/NoSQL databases, external or internal services).
11.2 Fetching data inside Server Components
11.3 Creating a reusable data service layer
lib/services/courseService.ts
app/courses/page.tsx
11.4 Connecting directly to a database
Important: Database credentials and database access modules must remain on the server. Use server-only module protections where appropriate.
11.5 Understanding caching
Caching stores previously retrieved or generated information so it can be reused, reducing repeated processing, database requests, latency, and infrastructure costs.
11.6 Types of caching concepts
Concept | Purpose
Request memoization | Reuses identical work within an individual render request
Data caching | Reuses previously retrieved data
Full route output caching | Reuses prerendered route output
Client Router Cache | Reuses route data during browser navigation
CDN caching | Distributes reusable responses closer to users
11.7 Understanding current Next.js fetch behavior

In the current previous-model documentation, fetch requests are not cached by default. Persistent caching can be configured explicitly. With Cache Components enabled, developers can also use "use cache" and cacheLife().
11.8 Server State vs Client State
State type | Category
Course catalogue | Server state
Database enrolment | Server state
Open navigation menu | Client state
Search input value | Client state
Saved student progress | Server state
Current modal visibility | Client state
11.9 Understanding TanStack Query
You must configure a QueryClientProvider in the appropriate Client Component provider.

Lesson outcome: You should be able to retrieve information from APIs and databases, build reusable data services, understand caching, distinguish server and client state, and choose an appropriate data-fetching strategy.
12.1 What is streaming?
Streaming is a rendering technique where the server sends parts of the response progressively rather than waiting for the entire page to finish rendering.
12.2 Traditional rendering vs streaming

Traditional all-at-once approach waits for the slowest request before sending the complete page. Streaming renders available content (such as Profile and Course List) immediately while slower sections (like Analytics) stream in when ready.
12.3 What is Suspense?
12.4 Creating an asynchronous Server Component
12.5 Understanding loading.tsx
app/dashboard/loading.tsx
Next.js uses this file to provide an automatic loading fallback for the route segment while shared layouts remain interactive. (Next.js)
12.6 Designing skeleton loading interfaces
12.7 Where should you use streaming?
Large dashboards, content feeds, search results, course catalogues, analytics pages, and pages retrieving data from multiple services with different loading times.
12.8 Understanding streaming limitations

Streaming does not automatically make a slow database query faster; it allows available content to become visible before slower work finishes. Infrastructure (servers, reverse proxies, CDNs) must preserve streaming behavior.
Lesson outcome: You should be able to implement Suspense boundaries, loading interfaces, skeleton screens and progressive server rendering.
13.1 What is metadata?
Metadata describes a webpage's content for browsers, search engines, and social platforms (page title, meta description, canonical URL, Open Graph, robots directives, icons).
13.2 Static metadata
app/about/page.tsx
13.3 Dynamic metadata
app/courses/[slug]/page.tsx
generateMetadata runs on the server and is not a Client Component export. (Next.js)
13.4 Understanding metadata inheritance
Layouts can define title templates:
13.5 Open Graph metadata
13.6 Technical SEO requirements
SEO element | Purpose
Title tag | Describes the page title
Meta description | Summarizes page content
Canonical URL | Identifies the preferred page URL
Robots meta | Controls indexing instructions
Sitemap | Helps search engines discover URLs
robots.txt | Provides crawling instructions
Open Graph | Controls supported social previews
Structured data | Helps describe entities and content
Internal links | Helps users and crawlers navigate the site
13.7 Sitemap and robots files
app/robots.ts
app/sitemap.ts
13.8 Important SEO distinction

Having metadata does not guarantee search engine indexing or ranking. You still need valuable original content, crawlable public URLs, canonical URLs, reliable server responses, mobile-friendly pages, good loading performance, and correct robots/indexing instructions.
Lesson outcome: You should be able to configure static and dynamic metadata, social previews, canonical URLs, robots directives and dynamic sitemaps.
14.1 Understanding image optimization
Image optimization involves choosing appropriate dimensions, compressing images, selecting modern formats, supporting responsive sizes, and preventing layout shifts.
14.2 Understanding next/image
Properties: src, alt, width, height, fill, sizes, priority / preload configuration.
14.3 Optimizing remote images
next.config.ts
14.4 Responsive image optimization

<Image
  src="/images/course.jpg"
  alt="Course illustration"
  width={1200}
  height={800}
  sizes="(max-width: 640px) 100vw, (max-width: 1024px) 50vw, 33vw"

14.5 Understanding Image formats
Format | Typical usage
JPEG | Photographs
PNG | Images requiring transparency
WebP | Optimized web images
AVIF | Modern image compression
SVG | Logos, icons and vector graphics
14.6 What is font optimization?
Poorly managed font loading can cause delayed text rendering, layout shifts, and extra network requests. Next.js provides next/font.
14.7 Using Google Fonts
14.8 Using local fonts
14.9 Performance considerations
Understand the relationship with Core Web Vitals: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), and Interaction to Next Paint (INP).

Lesson outcome: You should be able to implement optimized images, configure remote images, manage responsive images, load custom fonts, and understand the relationship between media optimization and web performance.

sections.title: Error Handling, Loading Interfaces and Not Found Pages

blocks.text: 15.1 Understanding application errors
1. Expected errors: Incorrect password, invalid form input, insufficient permissions, course not found, payment declined.
2. Unexpected errors: Database connection failure, unexpected runtime exception, invalid external service response, rendering failure.
15.2 Understanding error.tsx
app/dashboard/error.tsx
Error boundaries must be Client Components. Server-side error details should be logged securely rather than exposed to visitors. (Next.js)
15.3 Understanding loading.tsx
app/courses/loading.tsx
15.4 Understanding not-found.tsx
app/courses/[slug]/not-found.tsx
15.5 Programmatically triggering not-found
15.6 Understanding the difference
File | Purpose
loading.tsx | Displays loading UI
error.tsx | Handles unexpected runtime errors
not-found.tsx | Handles missing pages or resources
global-error.tsx | Handles root-level errors
15.7 Designing production-grade error experiences
Provide clear, reassuring feedback with recovery actions, plus server-side error logging, error monitoring, retry behavior, timeout handling, and duplicate submission prevention.
Lesson outcome: You should be able to implement loading states, route-level error boundaries, not-found handling, recovery interfaces and secure error reporting.
16.1 What is deployment?
Deployment is the process of making an application available in a production environment (Write Code -> Test -> Push to Git -> Build -> Deploy -> Production Website).
16.2 Understanding the Next.js production build
Run npm run build to generate an optimized production build, then npm run start to start the production server. Always test the production build before launching.
16.3 Understanding deployment architecture

Users
                   ↓
                Internet
                   ↓
              CDN / Proxy
                   ↓
          Next.js Application
     ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
     ↓             ↓             ↓
Server Rendering  Cache     Static Assets
                   ↓
              Data Layer
             ┌─────┴─────┐
             ↓           ↓
         Database   External APIs
16.4 Deployment options
Hosting platforms include Vercel, Amazon Web Services (containers/servers/managed services), Docker, Cloudflare, and self-hosted Node.js servers.
16.5 Understanding Node.js deployment

npm install
npm run build
npm run start
The Next.js documentation identifies a Node.js server as the baseline for supporting the framework's full feature set, including Server Components, ISR and Server Actions. (Next.js)
16.6 Understanding Docker deployment

FROM node:22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=builder /app ./
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "run", "start"]
A production implementation should use a non-root user, a minimal runtime image and only the necessary build artifacts and dependencies.
16.7 Environment variables in production
Never place production secrets inside public source repositories, frontend JavaScript, public environment variables, or client-side configuration files.
16.8 Understanding production caching

When deploying multiple Next.js instances behind a CDN, independent local caches may temporarily serve different versions. Production systems with multiple instances may need shared cache storage, cache coordination, consistent tag invalidation, and appropriate CDN configuration. (Next.js)
16.9 Static export vs full Next.js deployment
Feature | Full server deployment | Static export
Static pages | Yes | Yes
Server Components | Yes | Build-time output only
Request-time SSR | Yes | No
ISR | Yes, with supported runtime | No
Server Actions | Yes, with supported runtime | No
Dynamic request-dependent data | Yes | No
Static assets | Yes | Yes
16.10 Production readiness checklist

Verify: production build succeeds, routes work, Server/Client Components are used appropriately, APIs and DB work, authentication is secure, env vars are configured, loading/error states work, metadata/images/fonts/caching behave as expected, mobile navigation works, and logs/monitoring are active.
Lesson outcome: You should understand production builds, hosting architectures, Node.js deployment, Docker, environment management, caching infrastructure and the limitations of static exports.
Major practical project
Project objective
Build a complete content-driven learning platform using Next.js, TypeScript and the App Router.
The application should demonstrate how a modern frontend framework handles routing, reusable layouts, content retrieval, server rendering, caching, SEO, loading states and deployment.
1. Application requirements

Course catalogue | /courses | Display available courses
Course details | /courses/[slug] | Display individual courses
Category pages | /categories/[slug] | Display courses by category
Article catalogue | /articles | Display educational articles
Article details | /articles/[slug] | Display individual articles
About page | /about | Platform information
Search page | /search | Search and filter content

3. Functional requirements
A. Course management: Retrieve courses from an API or database, display course cards, implement dynamic course URLs, display descriptions/levels, implement category filtering.
B. Article management: Retrieve educational articles, generate dynamic article pages, display content and publication info, generate metadata per article.
C. Search functionality: Search interface, query parameters, filter courses and articles, empty-result and loading states.
D. Rendering architecture: Server Components for content retrieval; Client Components for interactive search inputs, filters, and menus.
E. SEO: Dynamic page titles, meta descriptions, canonical URLs, Open Graph metadata, sitemap generation, robots configuration.
F. User experience: Responsive layout, loading skeletons, error boundaries, custom not-found interfaces, optimized images and fonts.
4. Rendering strategy for the project
Page | Recommended approach
Homepage | Static or cached rendering
Course catalogue | Static or cached rendering
Course details | SSG with revalidation where suitable
Article details | SSG with revalidation where suitable
Search | Dynamic or interactive client-side retrieval
Authenticated dashboard extension | Request-specific rendering
A critical requirement is that private, user-specific information must never be placed in a shared public cache.
5. Required engineering tasks
1. Initialize a Next.js TypeScript application — Configure App Router, project dependencies and development scripts.
2. Create the application folder architecture — Separate pages, layouts, components, services and TypeScript types.
3. Build reusable layouts and navigation — Implement root layout, nested layouts and route navigation.
4. Implement dynamic routes — Build course and article pages using dynamic slugs.
5. Connect the data layer — Retrieve course and article content through reusable data services.
6. Implement rendering strategies — Demonstrate static generation and request-time rendering.
7. Implement caching and revalidation — Configure caching for public content and update it after content changes.
8. Implement streaming and Suspense — Display independently loading page sections.
9. Implement metadata and SEO — Add dynamic metadata, social previews, sitemap and robots.
10. Optimize images and fonts — Use next/image, remotePatterns and next/font.
11. Implement error handling — Add loading, not-found and error interfaces.
12. Prepare production deployment — Verify builds, environment variables, performance and hosting.
6. Final project evaluation
Evaluation area | Expected result

SEO | Correct dynamic metadata

Reliability | Error and not-found handling
Deployment | Successful production build and deployment
Final deliverable: A working, production-buildable Next.js content platform with documented architectural decisions and source code.

Important course-version note: This module follows the modern App Router documentation, checked against the Next.js documentation updated in 2026. In particular, students must understand asynchronous route parameters and the distinction between the previous caching model and the newer optional Cache Components architecture. They should not blindly copy examples from older Next.js tutorials.
What students should be able to build after this module
Content platforms: Courses, articles and documentation systems.
SaaS applications: Dynamic dashboards and authenticated interfaces.
E-commerce: Product catalogues, dynamic pages and metadata.
Documentation systems: Searchable documentation and static content.

Completion standard: Students should not merely know Next.js syntax. They should be able to explain why a page uses Server Components, whether its content should be statically generated or dynamically rendered, how its data is cached, how its metadata is generated, and how the whole application reaches production.
